# Skills overview

## What is a "skill"?

A **skill** is a reusable, model-agnostic workflow an AI coding agent loads
on demand:

- A `SKILL.md` file — step-by-step instructions for one class of task
- Supporting **reference files** — conventions, function-selection logic,
  failure modes
- Bundled **scripts** — R / Python the agent runs in your environment

The agent reads the skill only when your request matches it, then follows it
instead of improvising.

::: {.notes}
Contrast with a raw prompt: a prompt is transient and lives in one person's
head or chat history. A skill is version-controlled, reviewable, and encodes
institutional knowledge — "here is how *we* derive ADSL" — so every run starts
from the same vetted baseline.

Analogy: an SOP that the agent actually executes, not just reads.
:::

## Why skills matter for clinical programming

Clinical programming is high-stakes, convention-heavy, and traceability-driven.
A skill lets you encode, once:

- CDISC / ADaMIG conventions (`"Y"`/`NA` flags, study-day rules, date
  imputation direction)
- Function-selection logic (when `derive_vars_merged()` vs
  `derive_vars_merged_lookup()`)
- QC scaffolding (`stopifnot()` assertions, `# REVIEW:` markers at every
  protocol-specific decision)

The agent then reproduces that discipline on every run.

::: {.notes}
The point is consistency and traceability, not just speed. A skilled run
produces code that already has review markers where a human must make a
protocol call — the reviewer's attention is directed, not diffused.
:::

From the repo root, run the environment check script:


It verifies, printing `[ OK ]` / `[WARN]` / `[FAIL]` per line:

- R &ge; 4.2 and the admiral set (`admiral` &ge; 1.2.0, `dplyr`, `lubridate`,

- The GSD set (`gsDesign`, `gsDesign2`, `lrstat`, `graphicalMCP`, `jsonlite`)

**All `[ OK ]` &rarr; you're ready.** Any `[FAIL]` &rarr; install commands are
in `README.md`.

::: {.notes}
`check_setup.R` is base-R only (no package needed to run it) and installs
nothing — it only reports. On Windows it skips the Microsoft Store
`python3.exe` alias and finds a real interpreter via `py -3`.

becomes a 10-second confirmation rather than an install step.

# Section A — ADaM generation {.unnumbered}

## Section A — what we'll do

Drive the **admiral** skill family to derive ADaM datasets from SDTM:

| Skill | Produces | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| `admiral` (parent) | Shared conventions — no output | — |
| `admiral-adsl` | ADSL (subject-level) | SDTM DM, EX, DS |
| `admiral-adae` | ADAE (adverse events, TEAE flag) | ADSL + SDTM AE |
| `admiral-bds` | ADVS / ADLB (BDS findings) | ADSL + SDTM VS / LB |

**ADSL must be derived first** — its treatment vars and population flags feed
every downstream dataset.

::: {.notes}
Source data is the pharmaverse public CDISC test data (`pharmaversesdtm` /
`pharmaverseadam`) — no proprietary data involved, safe to run live.

The agent reads `skills/admiral/SKILL.md` (shared conventions) first, then the
child skill for the dataset in question.

[CONFIRM WITH JEFF: time budget for Section A.]
:::

## Section A — how the skill behaves

When you ask for a derivation, the skilled agent will:

- Generate code **section by section**, not one giant block
- Use the native pipe `|>` and `exprs()` for admiral verb arguments
- Use admiral date functions (never `as.Date()` on `--DTC`)
- Emit `"Y"`/`NA` flags — never `"N"`
- Drop a **`# REVIEW:`** comment at every protocol-specific decision
- Add `stopifnot()` assertions (one row per USUBJID, source uniqueness, …)

::: {.notes}
Tell attendees what to look for when reviewing: the `# REVIEW:` markers are
where *they* — not the agent — own the decision (population flag definitions,
disposition mapping, age cut-points, TEAE window). The skill deliberately does
not guess these.
:::

# Section B — Group sequential design {.unnumbered}

## Section B — what we'll do

Drive the **group-sequential-design** skill to design a survival trial:

- Survival endpoints (OS / PFS / DFS), interim + final analyses
- Alpha-spending boundaries (Lan-DeMets, Hwang-Shih-DeCani)
- Sample-size / event targets (N-first approach)
- Graphical multiplicity for co-primary / multi-population designs
- **`lrstat` simulation** to verify the analytic design
- A template-driven **Word report** (`gsd_report.py`)

::: {.notes}
Scope note the skill enforces: standard group sequential designs only. Adaptive
enrichment, sample-size re-estimation, seamless dose-selection, platform trials,
and non-survival primary endpoints are explicitly out of scope — the skill will
say so and stop.

Tools: gsDesign, gsDesign2, lrstat, graphicalMCP, jsonlite (R) + python-docx.

[CONFIRM WITH ERIC: time budget for Section B.]
:::

## Section B — how the skill behaves

- Asks design questions **one at a time**, in plain language, no defaults
  offered
- Summarises all inputs in a table and waits for your confirmation
- Computes the design, then **checks interim-analysis timing** against
  enrollment and minimum-gap constraints
- **Verifies by simulation** before delivering — power within ±2 pp, type I
  error within ±0.5 pp
- Writes every number to `gsd_results.json`; the report reads from there (no
  hardcoded values)

::: {.notes}
The one-artifact-per-turn pacing in the skill means the agent writes a script,
stops, runs it, stops, etc. That is intentional — it keeps each step
reviewable.
:::

::: {.notes}

:::

## Disclaimer

These skills produce **drafting aids, not validated deliverables**.

LLM output can be wrong or vary between runs. Independently verify all
generated code and results against your own QC process before they inform any
regulatory, clinical, safety, or GxP-regulated activity, and comply with your
organization's policies.

The skills bundle scripts that execute in your environment — review a skill's
contents before running it, and only supply data you are permitted to use.
